subject: Anatomy
summary: The hip joint is a ball‑and‑socket synovial joint that allows a wide range of motion while bearing weight. Its stability depends on bony congruence, ligaments, capsule, and surrounding muscles. Clinically, injury or degeneration alters gait and pain patterns.

sections.p: The hip joint connects the femur to the pelvis, forming a stable yet mobile structure essential for locomotion. Its design balances strength and flexibility, making it vulnerable to mechanical overload and neurovascular injury.
The femoral head fits into the acetabulum of the ilium, ischium, and pubis. The joint capsule is reinforced by the iliofemoral, pubofemoral, and ischiofemoral ligaments.
Anteriorly the femoral neurovascular bundle passes; posteriorly the sciatic nerve lies. The joint is surrounded by gluteus medius/minimus, iliopsoas, and adductors.
The femoral head receives blood from the medial and lateral femoral circumflex arteries, with the medial branch being most critical.
Innervation is via the femoral nerve (anterior), obturator nerve (medial), and superior gluteal nerve (posterior).
Provides flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, and internal/external rotation. It supports upright posture and transfers weight to the lower limb.

Common problems include osteoarthritis, avascular necrosis, dislocation, and superior gluteal nerve injury. In low‑resource settings, infections like septic arthritis and trauma from falls or road traffic accidents are frequent.
b: Avascular necrosis: sudden pain, collapse of femoral head

t.b: Shows joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis – indicates osteoarthritis or fracture
Detects early cartilage loss, AVN, or soft tissue injury – useful when X‑ray is inconclusive
Assesses bursitis or effusion when MRI unavailable

sections.p: Ask about gait pattern, pain location, and history of trauma. Look for Trendelenburg sign to assess gluteus medius function. In suspected dislocation, check for limb shortening and external rotation.
b: Trendelenburg sign – positive if hip drops on contralateral side

sections.p: Treat underlying cause: anti‑inflammatories for arthritis, antibiotics for septic arthritis, surgical reduction for dislocation. Supportive care includes pain control, physiotherapy, and weight management.
b: Antibiotics – cover Staph aureus, Gram‑negative rods

sections.p: Differential includes lumbar radiculopathy, sacroiliitis, and hip osteochondritis dissecans. Clinical history and imaging help distinguish them.
b: Lumbar radiculopathy – pain radiates to leg, improves with flexion

sections.p: Early osteoarthritis may show normal X‑ray; inflammatory markers can be normal in septic arthritis if infection is low‑grade.
b: Normal CRP in early septic arthritis

whenToSeekHelp: Severe sudden hip pain with inability to bear weight

faq.a: Weakness of gluteus medius/minimus due to superior gluteal nerve injury or muscle degeneration.

faq.q: Why is the femoral head at risk of avascular necrosis?
faq.a: Its blood supply is precarious; trauma or prolonged steroid use can interrupt the medial femoral circumflex artery.

faq.q: How does osteoarthritis present differently in the hip than the knee?
faq.a: Hip OA pain is deep, worsens with prolonged standing, and improves with rest; knee OA pain is more localized to joint line.

exam: Explain how the acetabulum’s depth contributes to hip stability.
Describe the clinical steps to reduce a posterior hip dislocation.
Identify the key ligaments that prevent anterior dislocation of the hip.
